prompt: A brigade commander in Mindanao wants a force that attacks mounted in protected vehicles, combines fire and maneuver at the decisive time and place, and may also be tasked with ISO in peacetime. Which assessment of armor is accurate?
options: Armor fights mainly dismounted, relies on maneuver alone, and is barred from ISO in peacetime
Armor fights as a pure tank force without other arms, relying on shock effect only, and may not conduct ISO
Armor fights mounted in armor-protected vehicles, uses controlled fire and maneuver, and may conduct ISO when higher headquarters requires
Armor fights from static positions, relies on indirect fire, and conducts ISO only in wartime
explanation: Pages 13-14 give the definition, the fire and maneuver method and the ISO provision.

prompt: A staff assigns three missions: (1) reconnaissance, surveillance and security; (2) neutralize the enemy by fire, maneuver and shock effect; (3) close with the enemy to destroy or capture him. Which units match, in order?
options: Tank, cavalry, mechanized infantry
Mechanized infantry, tank, cavalry
Cavalry, mechanized infantry, tank
Cavalry, tank, mechanized infantry
explanation: Pages 16-18 give these three missions.

prompt: An S3 argues that armor operations succeed through shock effect alone. Which flaw does the lesson expose?
options: Shock effect is not part of the armor mission, which depends only on dismounted fire and maneuver
Armor operations depend on armor protection alone, so firepower and mobility are secondary
Shock effect applies only to cavalry, so tanks and mechanized infantry should not seek it
Armor operations combine and control fire and maneuver to create a preponderance of combat power, with shock effect applied in coordination with other arms
explanation: Pages 13-14 tie shock effect to fire and maneuver in coordination with other arms.

prompt: After an exercise, a company is scored: crews survived small arms and shell fragments, the radio net failed during maneuver, and the vehicles kept pace over varied terrain. Which assessment fits the lesson?
options: Armor protection was degraded, intensive and flexible communication held, and mobility held
Armor protection held, intensive and flexible communication was degraded, and mobility held
Armor protection held, intensive and flexible communication held, and mobility was degraded
Armor protection and mobility were degraded, while intensive and flexible communication held
explanation: Page 20 names all three characteristics.

prompt: A planner links vehicle features to characteristics: the 25 mm cannon, the amphibious M113A2 hull, and Level 4 ballistic protection on the Sabrah. Which linkage is correct?
options: Mobility, firepower, armor protection
Armor protection, mobility, firepower
Firepower, armor protection, mobility
Firepower, mobility, armor protection
explanation: Pages 20, 73, 75 and 82 support this linkage.

prompt: A mechanized infantry platoon has 1 officer and 37 enlisted; the HQ has 1 officer and 10 enlisted and the three squads are equal. How many enlisted are in each squad, and how many AIFVs does the platoon use?
options: 12 enlisted per squad; three AIFVs
9 enlisted per squad; four AIFVs
10 enlisted per squad; four AIFVs
9 enlisted per squad; three AIFVs
explanation: Page 25 gives 37 - 10 = 27, or 9 per squad; page 27 gives four AIFVs.

prompt: During a dismount, who is responsible for both the maneuver of the dismount team and the positioning of the AV?
options: The squad leader or the platoon leader
The AIFV driver alone
The carrier team leader only
The company first sergeant
explanation: Page 31 assigns this responsibility to the SL or PL.

prompt: A mechanized infantry company has three platoons of four AIFVs each. How many AIFVs do the platoons field together?
options: Eight
Ten
Twelve
Sixteen
explanation: Pages 24 and 27 give three platoons of four AIFVs each: 3 x 4 = 12.

prompt: A platoon must assault unprepared, suppressed defenses, infiltrate along a trail vehicles cannot use, and fix the enemy so tanks can maneuver. Which allocation matches the lesson?
options: Assault dismounted; infiltrate mounted; fix mounted
Assault mounted; infiltrate and fix dismounted
Assault, infiltrate and fix all mounted
Assault, infiltrate and fix all dismounted
explanation: Pages 28-29 list the mounted and dismounted capabilities.

prompt: Enemy mortars range the only road while AIFVs halt so squads can dismount. Which limitations combine here?
options: AVs are restricted to certain avenues, infantry need time to mount and dismount, and dismounted infantry are vulnerable to indirect fire
AIFVs are less vulnerable than tanks, infantry dismount instantly, and indirect fire is no risk
AVs may use any avenue, infantry need no time to dismount, and small arms are the only risk
AIFVs and APCs are stronger than tanks, so halting is safe, and dismounted infantry are protected by armor
explanation: Page 30 lists all three limitations.

prompt: A commander says mechanized infantry are tanks with legs and will lead an assault against enemy tanks. Which flaw does the lesson show?
options: Mechanized infantry should lead because AIFVs are better protected than tanks
Mechanized infantry can be used against tank units if the infantry stay dismounted
Mechanized infantry cannot be used against tank units, and AIFVs and APCs are more vulnerable than tanks
Mechanized infantry lack the firepower to support tanks in any form of attack
explanation: Pages 30 and 69 give both points.

prompt: A squad dismounts left because terrain on the right is unfavorable, and fire opens from the right as it deploys. Which actions follow?
options: Return fire from the kill zone, remain there until the AV is repositioned, then dismount the rest
Dismount right into the enemy fire, then wait for the AV to reposition before reacting
Stay mounted, close the ramp and wait until the enemy fire ceases before the dismount drill
React to contact on the right, extricate out of the kill zone, perform IAD after dismount procedures, with the SL or PL positioning the AV
explanation: Pages 31 and 35-39 combine the dismount left objectives with the SOP on positioning the AV.

prompt: A squad remounts from the right while under fire from the left. Which actions comply with the SOPs?
options: Rush the door together, keep weapons loaded and muzzles up inside, and close the ramp after the last soldier
Provide cover while others mount, avoid piling at the door, move in one at a time, clear weapons and muzzles down inside
Mount only after the enemy fire stops, then climb on top of the AV to watch the flank
Let the first soldiers out board first, hide behind the AV, then board when the cover team is ready
explanation: Pages 45 and 49 combine the mounting SOPs with mounting from the right under fire from the left.

prompt: Eight soldiers dismounted in order 1 through 8 and must remount under fire. Which sequence follows the SOPs?
options: Soldier 8 mounts first, soldier 1 mounts last, one at a time, with cover provided
Soldier 1 mounts first and soldier 8 last, all in a single rush
All eight mount at once to save time, in any order
Soldier 1 mounts first and soldier 8 last, one at a time
explanation: Page 31 says the first to dismount is last to mount and vice versa; page 45 says one at a time with cover.

prompt: A brigade commander gives a cavalry troop a zone reconnaissance as flank guard while keeping the main body concentrated for the decisive point. Which fundamentals support this?
options: Main effort, concealment from the enemy, and permanent holding of the flank
Rear security, resupply of the main body, and replacement of the reserve
Economy of force, eyes and ears for situational awareness, and concentration of superior combat power at the decisive time and point
Reserve role, counterattack, and reinforcement of the main body
explanation: Pages 53-54 and 60 support these fundamentals.

prompt: A separate cavalry troop with a light brigade must cover a flank through dense forest, steep ridges and a major river, with a stretched supply line. Which statement fits the lesson?
options: It works for the division commander as a heavy unit, and terrain does not restrict its mobility
It works for the brigade commander as a heavy unit, since all separate troops are heavy
It works for the division commander as a light unit, and logistics are not a concern
It works for the brigade commander as a light unit, but high logistics needs and terrain-restricted mobility are limitations
explanation: Pages 58 and 61 give these points.

prompt: A unit supporting a separate light brigade needs the cavalry design organized as part of that brigade. Which design is it?
options: Cavalry Troop/Company (Separate), light because the brigade is light
Cavalry Squadron/Battalion, heavy because squadrons are always heavy
Air Cavalry Squadron, light because it flies above the brigade
Cavalry Troop/Company, assigned to the division and not to the brigade
explanation: Pages 55 and 58 describe the separate troop and its weight.

prompt: A tank company is attached to an infantry battalion for a theater deployment. Which arrangements does the lesson require?
options: The tanks deploy under their own power, and the infantry trucks carry all Class III, V and IX supplies
The tanks deploy by air, and the infantry battalion provides all Class III, V and IX support
Flatbeds for deployment, and FFSU and division CSS support for Classes III, V and IX because the infantry lacks organic transport
The tanks need no sustainment support, since they carry enough supplies for the whole operation
explanation: Pages 67-68 give the flatbed and CSS limitations.

prompt: A light tank must fight in extremely close terrain against infantry with anti-armor weapons and antitank mines. Which statement fits the lesson?
options: Light tanks lack main battle tank protection, are vulnerable to anti-armor weapons and mines, and their mobility and firepower are restricted in close terrain
Light tanks match main battle tank protection and can ignore mines, but mobility is restricted
Light tanks are protected against all anti-armor weapons, and close terrain improves their firepower
Light tanks are vulnerable only to enemy aircraft, and close terrain improves their mobility
explanation: Pages 67-68 list these limitations.

prompt: A tank platoon leader plans an SBF and asks about employment. Which statement is correct?
options: Plan the objective to combat trains distance and the Ex-O as resource manager; tanks cannot be used against other tanks
Plan the surface danger zone, direct fire control measures and cover against enemy air; tanks may be used against other tanks or any armored vehicle
Plan indirect fire weapon support and distance from main body; tanks should be kept from armored vehicles
Plan where to dismount and avenue restrictions; tanks may be used only against infantry
explanation: Page 71 lists tank planning considerations.

prompt: A task force commander gives four assignments. Which one violates the lesson's planning considerations?
options: The cavalry troop screens at a planned distance from the main body
The mechanized infantry company attacks the enemy tank company
The tank platoon occupies an SBF position with cover against enemy air
The mechanized infantry commander plans where to dismount on, before or after the objective
explanation: Page 69 says mechanized infantry cannot be used against tank units; the other assignments follow pages 69-71.

prompt: A staff matches considerations to units: Ex-O as resource manager and objective-to-combat-trains distance; indirect fire weapon support and distance from main body; surface danger zone and SBF positions. Which units, in order?
options: Cavalry, tank, mechanized infantry
Tank, mechanized infantry, cavalry
Mechanized infantry, cavalry, tank
Mechanized infantry, tank, cavalry
explanation: Pages 69-71 list the considerations per unit.

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: A planner needs wheeled vehicles only for a road march. Which group contains only wheeled vehicles from the lesson?
options: M113A2 APC, Simba Fighting Vehicle and Guarani 6x6
Commando V-150S, Sabrah Light Tank and Guarani 6x6
Commando V-150S, Simba Fighting Vehicle and Guarani 6x6
Commando V-150S, Fire Support Vehicle and Simba Fighting Vehicle
explanation: Pages 79, 80 and 83 describe wheeled vehicles; the M113A2 family (page 73), FSV and Sabrah are tracked.

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: A target sits 3,200 m away. Which vehicle can engage it within its stated maximum effective range?
options: Sabrah Light Tank ASCOD II (3,600 m)
M113A2 IFV Unmanned Turret System (3,000 m)
Fire Support Vehicle (2,200 m direct fire)
Guarani 6x6 wheeled APC (1,830 m)
explanation: Pages 75, 81, 82 and 83 give these effective ranges.

category: Major Equipment of the Armor Division
prompt: A commander needs casualty evacuation, 81/120 mm mortar fire, and 76 mm direct fire support. Which vehicles fit, in order?
options: Mounted Mortar System, M113A2 APC (ambulance), Fire Support Vehicle
Fire Support Vehicle, Mounted Mortar System, M113A2 APC (ambulance)
M113A2 APC (ambulance), Fire Support Vehicle, Mounted Mortar System
M113A2 APC (ambulance), Mounted Mortar System, Fire Support Vehicle
explanation: Pages 77, 78 and 81 describe these vehicles.
